answers.answer: Replication copies data changes between servers; each maintained copy is a replica. It keeps the same data in several places, whereas sharding divides data into different groups; each group can itself have replicas. Copies can serve reads and take over failed-server responsibilities, but routing and safe takeover must be designed separately. Lag can make reads old, and extra read replicas do not automatically increase write capacity. A new replica commonly starts with a snapshot, a database copy at a known point, then receives a change log recording subsequent source changes. Applying changes updates replica data so queries see them, preserving required source order. The snapshot and starting log position must agree to avoid missing or incorrectly applying changes. Receipt alone may leave changes unapplied and therefore invisible.

evidence.quote: Copies data changes between servers. Each maintained copy is a replica.
Read routing and a safe takeover process are separate design work; a second copy does not configure either automatically.
The initial copy and starting log position must agree. Otherwise the handoff can miss changes or apply them incorrectly.
The replica updated its data so queries can see the change.

answers.answer: Asynchronous replication allows the writing server to acknowledge success before another replica confirms the change. Acknowledgement says the configured success condition was met, not that another server has the data. If the primary acknowledges a write, permanently fails before sending it, and a replica takes over, that replica lacks the confirmed write. Avoiding the replica wait lowers write waiting time but permits stale reads and recent-write loss. Synchronous replication waits for required replica confirmations. Specify the replica set or count and stage: received may mean only memory, durable storage survives restart, and applied means visible to queries. Waiting for durable copies protects against writing-server loss but adds delay; writes can stall when too few required replicas respond, unlike asynchronous writes that need not wait for replica confirmation. Synchronous success need not involve every replica or wait for application, so every replica read need not be current. It does not protect against losing every copy or unwanted logical changes.

evidence.quote: The writing server can acknowledge success before a replica confirms the change. Acknowledgement means the configured success condition was met, not that every copy has the data.
If the writing server fails permanently before sending a confirmed change, a replacement replica will not have that change.
Choose the required replica set or count and acknowledgement stage. This protects against specified failures, not loss of every copy or accidental logical changes.
Waiting for durable copies protects against losing the writing server. It adds delay, and writes can stall if too few required replicas respond.

answers.answer: Replication lag means a replica is behind in receiving or applying source changes. A successful write can be followed by an old replica read because the replica has not applied the update. Read-your-writes means later reads include your completed change or newer state. Reading the still-authoritative primary holding that write avoids waiting for replica application but concentrates load and requires correct authority after failover. Waiting for evidence the chosen replica applied that particular write adds delay and can fail; a fixed sleep or low average lag is insufficient. Accepting old reads suits delay-tolerant work and permits replica read capacity without that freshness wait. None of these routing choices recovers a write already lost during failover. A leader accepts writes; with one leader per data set, followers copy its ordered changes and replacing it requires failover. Multiple leaders accept writes and exchange changes, potentially near users, but independent updates to the same item require conflict rules; latest timestamp can discard a valid edit. In leaderless arrangements any coordinator sends requests to data-holding replicas, waits for configured reply counts and repairs differences. Concurrent versions still need reconciliation. More write-accepting servers do not guarantee conflict-free updates or one current value.

evidence.quote: A replica is behind the source in receiving or applying changes. State which stage a lag measurement describes; data received but not applied is not yet visible to reads.
Primary reads concentrate load and require correct authority after failover. Waiting for a replica adds delay and can fail. Routing alone cannot recover a write already lost during failover.
One server accepts writes for a set of data. Followers copy its changes.
Concurrent versions still need reconciliation; no topology name guarantees one current value or conflict-free updates.

answers.answer: Failover moves a failed server's responsibilities to another. Promotion makes the selected replica the leader. Split brain is two servers each acting as sole leader and potentially accepting conflicting changes. Silence can mean a broken network connection while the old leader still accepts writes. Select a suitable replica whose progress meets recent-write survival needs, fence the old leader by preventing further writes, and redirect application connections to the replacement. Acknowledged asynchronous writes absent from that replacement may be lost. A healthy replica can copy an accidental deletion, so current replicated data is not an earlier recoverable state. A backup preserves earlier state; restoring it and replaying retained logs to just before deletion can recover that state. Retention and available logs limit history. A restore test must reconstruct usable application data and measure recovery duration. Neither an untested backup nor a current replica proves recoverable history or recovery time. Gap: the lesson does not give a concrete eligibility algorithm or precise progress threshold for choosing the replacement; those remain design work against recovery requirements.

evidence.quote: Moves a failed server's responsibilities to another server. In a single-leader system, the process selects a suitable replica, promotes it to leader, and redirects application connections.
A missing response does not prove the old leader stopped. Its network connection can be broken while it still accepts writes.
Replication also copies unwanted changes. If someone deletes the wrong records, replicas can apply that deletion too.
Retention and available logs bound recoverable history. Restore tests must reconstruct usable application data and measure how long recovery takes; file existence alone proves neither.

answers.answer: First establish acceptable acknowledged-write loss, how stale reporting may be, whether other reads require read-your-writes, acceptable write delay, recovery time or downtime, specified failures to survive, and required historical recovery period. A conditional policy is a single writing leader with synchronous durable acknowledgement from a specified replica set or count sufficient for those failure requirements. This narrows writing-server-loss exposure while adding commit delay and dependence on responding replicas; receipt alone is weaker and durable acknowledgement alone does not ensure query visibility. Route delay-tolerant reporting to replicas; use the authoritative primary or wait for application of a specific write where freshness matters. Prepare suitable up-to-date replacement selection, fencing and connection redirection, then exercise failover against recovery targets. Keep backups and saved logs for historical recovery and test restoration to usable application data with measured duration. Monitor progress, lag with its receive/apply stage, health and write waits, and account for storage, network and operating work. Replication alone specifies neither acknowledgements nor safe takeover nor historical recovery. Loss of all copies and unwanted replicated changes remain possible; when required copies are unreachable, agreement-dependent writes must wait or fail. Gap: no exact replica count, timing target or configuration can be chosen until the stated tolerances and failure scope are supplied.

evidence.quote: Choose acceptable acknowledged-write loss, read freshness, write latency and recovery time before choosing replica settings.

Delay-tolerant reads can use replicas. Freshness-sensitive reads need suitable routing or progress checks. Waiting for durable replica acknowledgements narrows some loss windows but adds commit delay and dependence on those replicas.
Copies consume storage, network and operating work. Monitor replication progress, lag, health and write waits; exercise failover and historical restore against the required recovery targets.
During a network split, operations that need agreement with unreachable copies must wait or fail.
